sections.title: Role, Value, and Challenges of Site Characterization
sections.summary: Site characterization informs geotechnical specialists and decision makers about ground conditions to identify and address risks. The fundamental value proposition: investigation costs are substantially less than costs of designing for uncertain conditions. Seven challenges make perfect characterization impossible: large volume vs. small volume sampled, inherent heterogeneity, complex mechanical behavior, unclear relative value of test choices, early-stage investigations before design details are set, groundwater variability, and practical constraints. The objective is acceptable characterization commensurate with risk and cost.
sections.body:
Characterization of subsurface conditions is one of the most challenging yet important activities for transportation infrastructure planning, design, construction, and operation. Risk is defined as potential for financial loss = probability of problem × cost of problem. Improved site characterization reduces risks by: (1) reducing likelihood of unforeseen conditions causing claims and change orders; (2) increasing reliability of design parameter estimates, reducing conservatism; and (3) reducing construction risks through better bid packages.

Seven challenges to effective site characterization: (1) volume sampled is very small compared to total volume; (2) materials are inherently heterogeneous; (3) mechanical behavior of soil/rock is complex and affected by many factors; (4) many different measurements can be made but their relative value is not quantitatively established; (5) investigations are performed early, before design details and loading conditions are established; (6) groundwater conditions vary over time; (7) access, regulatory, and budget constraints limit measurements. Because perfect site characterization is impossible, the objective is to characterize to an acceptable level commensurate with the value proposition — where cost savings from investigations exceed investigation costs.
key_points: Risk = probability of problem × financial cost; site characterization reduces both factors
Fundamental value proposition: investigation costs << costs of designing for uncertain conditions
Perfect site characterization is impossible; objective is acceptable level relative to risk and cost
7 challenges include: small sample volume, heterogeneity, complex behavior, unclear test value, early stage, GWT variability, practical constraints
sections.applicability: Framework for planning and justifying site characterization programs

sections.title: Purpose and Organization
sections.summary: GEC-5 improves site characterization practice among agencies, consultants, and contractors. It is a comprehensive reference for planning investigations and interpreting data to develop reliable design parameters. The manual is organized: Ch2 objectives/products; Ch3 planning and scoping; Ch4 soil/rock classification; Ch5 problematic geomaterials; Ch6-10 property interpretation (consolidation, strength, stiffness, rock, hydraulic); Ch11 design parameter selection; Ch12 geotechnical hazards; Ch13 documentation. Three appendices: ASTM/AASHTO standards, site characterization examples, variability/uncertainty quantification methods.
sections.body:
The objective of GEC-5 is to improve site characterization practices. The manual serves as a comprehensive reference for planning and executing geotechnical investigations and interpreting data to develop reliable design parameters. The manual is not prescriptive but provides guidance for: identifying and characterizing geotechnical hazards; interpreting soil and rock properties from field and laboratory measurements; and establishing reliable values for geotechnical design parameters from collective interpretation. The manual addresses LRFD design practice and explicit risk/reliability considerations, including methods to quantify variability and uncertainty in design parameters.

Organization: Ch2 — objectives, products, uses; Ch3 — planning and scoping (value of measurements, remote sensing, scoping guidelines); Ch4 — soil and rock classification; Ch5 — problematic geomaterials; Ch6 — consolidation properties; Ch7 — shear strength; Ch8 — stress-strain and stiffness; Ch9 — rock properties; Ch10 — hydraulic properties and groundwater; Ch11 — design parameter selection from collective measurements; Ch12 — geotechnical hazards (karst, mines, seismic, landslides, landfills); Ch13 — documentation and reporting. Three appendices: ASTM/AASHTO standards, site characterization examples, and variability/uncertainty quantification.
key_points: Provides guidance for planning investigations, interpreting properties, and selecting design parameters
Addresses LRFD design context and explicit quantification of variability and uncertainty in design parameters
Ch6-10: property interpretation (consolidation, strength, stiffness, rock, hydraulic) per individual test
Ch11: design parameter selection from collections of measurements — the culmination of site characterization
Appendix 3: methods for quantifying variability and uncertainty
